# Stretch Exercise

## Question 1a

The data combine [Demographic and Health Surveys](https://dhsprogram.com/) records with SPEI drought measures and IFPRI MapSPAM crop data. Each row is a living child under age five with a valid height measure and cluster location. The data cover child and household traits, maternal characteristics, drought exposure, crops, and geography. We predict whether a child is stunted (`haz < -2`) to help guide nutrition screening and support in Sub-Saharan Africa.

## Question 1b

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(rdhs)
library(sf)
library(terra)
library(haven)
library(tidymodels)
library(vip)
library(parsnip)

kids_merged <- readRDS("kids_merged.rds")
kids_merged$stunted <- factor(kids_merged$stunted, levels = c("yes", "no"))

set.seed(103)

split <- initial_split(
  kids_merged, 
  prop = 0.75,
  strata = stunted
) # Strata ensures that there is an even proportional share of stunted kids in training and testing data

kids_train <- training(x = split) 

kids_test <- testing(x = split)
```

### Data split and target

The file has 170,155 children from surveys conducted between 2012 and 2025. The target is `stunted`: “yes” when height-for-age z-score (`haz`) is below −2, and “no” otherwise. This binary outcome fits the screening goal. The file has 54,086 stunted children (31.8%) and 116,069 not stunted children (68.2%).

The code makes a reproducible, stratified 75/25 split. Stratifying keeps the share of stunted children similar in both sets. I use the training set for exploration and model selection, then evaluate the chosen model on the held-out test set.

The plots and summaries below use only the training set. The codebook explains that second-year drought measures are missing for many children who were not yet 12 months old. `rainfed_share` is missing where there is no harvested cropland. These missing values have known reasons, so I keep the records and impute predictors within each training fold. The codebook also documents how special DHS codes and derived variables were handled.

### Question 1d — Error metric and cost of errors

A false negative means a stunted child is predicted not stunted. This is more costly than a false positive because it may delay support. For this model, we will be focusing on ROC AUC as an error metric.

## Question 2a — Candidate model specifications

All three models predict `stunted`. I leave out `haz` and `hw70` because they define the target and would reveal the answer. I impute missing values, convert categories to indicator columns, and standardize numeric predictors for penalized logistic regression. Tree models do not need standardization. Preprocessing is learned within each training fold.

1.  **Non-survey context model:** `LATNUM`, `LONGNUM`, `ALT_DEM`, `URBAN_RURA`, the four `spei_mean_*` measures, four `drought_share_*` measures, `crop_ha_mean`, `staple_ha_mean`, `rainfed_ha`, and `rainfed_share`. Median-impute numeric values, one-hot encode `URBAN_RURA`, and standardize numeric predictors for logistic regression. Candidate algorithms are L1-penalized logistic regression (tune the penalty) and a CART tree (tune cost-complexity).

2.  **Survey household and child model:** `age_months`, `male`, `twin`, `first_birth`, `birth_int`, `birth_wt_kg`, `size_birth`, `mom_age_birth`, `mom_height_cm`, `mom_bmi`, `mom_educ_yrs`, `partner_educ`, `has_partner`, `child_deaths`, `wealth_z`, `improved_water`, `water_mins`, `improved_toilet`, `shared_toilet`, `clean_fuel`, `electricity`, `tv`, `fridge`, `finished_floor`, `urban`, `hh_size`, `n_under5`, `female_head`, `head_age`, `owns_land`, `distance_problem`, and `insured`. Median-impute numeric values, encode categorical values, and standardize numeric predictors for logistic regression. Candidate algorithms are L1-penalized logistic regression and random forest (tune split and leaf-size settings).

3.  **Combined model:** all predictors in the first two models, with the same imputation, encoding, and scaling. Candidate algorithms are L1-penalized logistic regression and random forest. Tune the penalty for logistic regression and the split and leaf-size settings for the forest.

Comparing the three models shows whether climate, crop, and geographic data add predictive value beyond household and child traits.

## Question 3a — Estimation on the training data

We use 10-fold stratified cross-validation to tune non-survey L1-penalized logistic regression. The latest script uses median imputation, dummy encoding, and normalization inside each fold. We use the training data to tune the model and keep the test data for final evaluation.

In the saved `result 2.RData` run, `lasso_best` selected a penalty of `1e-10`. Its 10-fold averages were ROC AUC **0.6111** (SD 0.0035), accuracy **0.6831** (SD 0.0012), and Brier score **0.2097** (SD 0.0005). Accuracy is close to the 68.2% majority-class benchmark, and the AUC shows modest separation. These numbers are from the saved run, which used KNN imputation; rerun cross-validation to get results for the latest median-imputation code.

The saved `lasso_coefs` ranks predictors by absolute coefficient size. The highest are `drought_share_rec` (0.262), `URBAN_RURA_U` (0.250), `LONGNUM` (0.228), `staple_ha_mean` (0.135), `LATNUM` (0.135), and `spei_mean_rec` (0.135). These are model associations, not causal effects. `lasso_final` is the finalized workflow; the code below fits it on the training data, creates the coefficient table, and reports test metrics.

```{r}
set.seed(103)

non_survey_rec <- recipe(
  stunted ~ LATNUM + LONGNUM + ALT_DEM + URBAN_RURA +
    spei_mean_utero + spei_mean_yr1 + spei_mean_yr2 + spei_mean_rec +
    drought_share_utero + drought_share_yr1 + drought_share_yr2 +
    drought_share_rec + crop_ha_mean + staple_ha_mean + rainfed_ha +
    rainfed_share,
  data = kids_train
) |>
  step_impute_median(all_numeric_predictors()) |>
  step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors()) |>
  step_normalize(all_predictors())

lasso_mod <- logistic_reg(penalty = tune(), mixture = 1) |>
  set_engine("glmnet")

lasso_wf <- workflow() |>
  add_recipe(non_survey_rec) |>
  add_model(lasso_mod)

set.seed(103)
folds <- vfold_cv(kids_train, v = 10, strata = stunted)
lasso_grid <- grid_regular(penalty(), levels = 10)

lasso_cv <- lasso_wf |>
  tune_grid(
    resamples = folds,
    grid = lasso_grid,
    control = control_grid(verbose = TRUE)
  )

lasso_best <- lasso_cv |>
  select_best(metric = "roc_auc")

lasso_final <- finalize_workflow(lasso_wf,  parameters = lasso_best
)

lasso_coefs <- lasso_fit |> #is this syntax correct? verify later!
  extract_fit_parsnip() |>
  vi(lambda = lasso_best$penalty)


```

## Non-survey predictors and preprocessing details

Variables included in the non-survey model:

All numeric variables get the same three recipe steps, in this order: missing values are filled with the training-data median or KNN (`step_impute_median()` or `step_impute_KNN()`), the categorical variable is turned into a 0/1 dummy (`step_dummy()`), and every predictor is centered and scaled to mean 0, SD 1 (`step_normalize()`) so LASSO penalizes them on the same scale. The notes below cover anything extra done to each variable.

- `LATNUM` Cluster latitude in decimal degrees (WGS84)
  - Clusters recorded at 0,0 (missing GPS) were dropped before modeling. Normalized in the recipe.
- `LONGNUM` Cluster longitude in decimal degrees (WGS84)
  - Same as latitude: missing-GPS clusters dropped, then normalized.
- `ALT_DEM` Cluster elevation in meters above sea level from Digital Elevation Model
  - Taken directly from the DHS GPS file. Normalized in the recipe. (DHS codes missing elevation as 9999, which should be set to `NA` before imputing.)
- `URBAN_RURA` Cluster urban/rural designation (`"U"` = Urban, `"R"` = Rural)
  - Converted to a single 0/1 dummy variable (rural is the reference category).
- `spei_mean_utero` Mean SPEI drought index in the 9 months before birth
  - SPEI was pulled at each cluster's location for every month, then averaged over this window for each child. Median-imputed and normalized.
- `spei_mean_yr1` Mean SPEI in the child's first year of life (months 0–11)
  - Same averaging as above. Median-imputed and normalized.
- `spei_mean_yr2` Mean SPEI in the child's second year of life (months 12–23)
  - Missing for children under 12 months, since this window hasn't happened yet. Those values are median-imputed, then normalized.
- `spei_mean_rec` Mean SPEI in the 12 months before the interview
  - Partly missing for surveys after December 2024, where SPEI data end. Median-imputed and normalized.
- `drought_share_utero` Share of months in drought (SPEI \< −1) in the 9 months before birth
  - Calculated as the proportion of months in the window below −1, so it runs from 0 to 1. Median-imputed and normalized.
- `drought_share_yr1` Share of months in drought in the first year of life
  - Same calculation as above. Median-imputed and normalized.
- `drought_share_yr2` Share of months in drought in the second year of life
  - Missing for children under 12 months. Median-imputed and normalized.
- `drought_share_rec` Share of months in drought in the 12 months before the interview
  - Same calculation. Median-imputed and normalized.
- `crop_ha_mean` Average harvested crop area (hectares) per MapSPAM cell within 10 km of the cluster
  - MapSPAM 2020 crop areas were summed across all crops, then averaged over a 10 km buffer around each cluster to account for DHS's GPS displacement. Normalized.
- `staple_ha_mean` Average harvested area of staple crops (cereals, roots, beans) within 10 km
  - Same buffer averaging, using staple crops only. Normalized.
- `rainfed_ha` Average rainfed harvested crop area within 10 km
  - Same buffer averaging, using MapSPAM's rainfed-only layer. Normalized.
- `rainfed_share` Share of harvested crop area that is rainfed (rainfed ÷ total)
  - Undefined (`NaN`) where a cluster has no cropland. Treated as missing, median-imputed, then normalized.

Variables included in the survey model:

These use the same recipe steps as the non-survey model (median imputation, dummy coding, normalization). Before the recipe, DHS special codes (e.g. 9996 "not weighed", 98 "don't know") were converted to `NA` in `data_script.R`, and categorical DHS codes were recoded into simple 0/1 indicators so they mean the same thing in every country.

- `age_months` Child's age in months (`hw1`)
  - No missing values. Normalized.
- `male` Child is male (1 = male, 0 = female; from `b4`)
  - Recoded from DHS codes to 0/1. Normalized.
- `twin` Child is a twin (from `b0`)
  - Recoded to 0/1 (any multiple birth = 1). Normalized.
- `bord` Birth order
  - Used as is. Normalized.
- `first_birth` Child is the mother's first birth
  - Created because the birth interval does not exist for first births. 0/1, normalized.
- `birth_int` Months since the previous birth (`b11`)
  - Set to 0 for first births, which `first_birth` flags. Normalized.
- `birth_wt_kg` Birth weight in kilograms (`m19`)
  - Codes 9996/9998 (not weighed, don't know) set to `NA`, then grams converted to kg. Only asked for recent births, so it has many missing values. Median-imputed, normalized.
- `size_birth` Mother's report of size at birth, 1 = very large to 5 = very small (`m18`)
  - "Don't know" set to `NA`. Median-imputed, normalized.
- `mom_age_birth` Mother's age at this child's birth, in years
  - Calculated from the child's and mother's birth dates (`b3 − v011`) and divided by 12. Normalized.
- `mom_height_cm` Mother's height in centimeters (`v438`)
  - Flag codes (9994+) set to `NA`, then converted from millimeters to centimeters. Some surveys only measured a subsample of mothers. Median-imputed, normalized.
- `mom_bmi` Mother's body mass index (`v445`)
  - Flag codes set to `NA`, then divided by 100. Median-imputed, normalized.
- `mom_educ_yrs` Mother's years of education (`v133`)
  - "Don't know" codes (97+) set to `NA`. Median-imputed, normalized.
- `has_partner` Mother is married or living with a partner (from `v501`)
  - Recoded to 0/1. Normalized.
- `partner_educ` Partner's years of education (`v715`)
  - Missing for mothers without a partner and for "don't know" answers. Median-imputed, normalized.
- `child_deaths` Number of the mother's children who have died (`v206` + `v207`)
  - Sons and daughters who died summed into one count. Normalized.
- `wealth_z` Household wealth index score (`v191`)
  - DHS builds the score separately for each country, so it was standardized *within each survey* to make it comparable across countries. Normalized.
- `urban` Urban residence (from `v025`)
  - Recoded to 0/1. Normalized.
- `hh_size` Number of household members (`v136`)
  - Used as is. Normalized.
- `n_under5` Number of children under 5 in the household (`v137`)
  - Used as is. Normalized.
- `female_head` Household head is female (from `v151`)
  - Recoded to 0/1. Normalized.
- `head_age` Age of household head (`v152`)
  - "Don't know" codes set to `NA`. Median-imputed, normalized.
- `improved_water` Household uses an improved drinking-water source (from `v113`)
  - Country-specific source codes grouped into improved/unimproved using the WHO/UNICEF definition. 0/1, normalized.
- `water_mins` Minutes to get to the water source (`v115`)
  - "On premises" (996) set to 0; "don't know" set to `NA`. Median-imputed, normalized.
- `improved_toilet` Household has an improved toilet (from `v116`)
  - Toilet codes grouped into improved/unimproved (WHO/UNICEF definition). 0/1, normalized.
- `shared_toilet` Toilet is shared with other households (`v160`)
  - Recoded to 0/1. Normalized.
- `clean_fuel` Household cooks with electricity, LPG, natural gas, or biogas (from `v161`)
  - Fuel codes grouped into clean vs. solid/other fuels. 0/1, normalized.
- `electricity`, `radio`, `tv`, `fridge` Household owns or has each item (`v119`–`v122`)
  - Each recoded to 0/1. Normalized.
- `finished_floor` Household has a finished floor (from `v127`)
  - Floor codes grouped: finished (codes 30–39) = 1, natural or rudimentary = 0. Normalized.
- `owns_land` Mother owns land alone or jointly (from `v745b`)
  - Recoded to 0/1. Missing in one survey, which is median-imputed. Normalized.
- `distance_problem` Distance to a health facility is a big problem for the mother (`v467d`)
  - Recoded to 0/1. Normalized.
- `insured` Mother has any health insurance (`v481`)
  - Recoded to 0/1. Normalized.

Country code (`cc`), cluster ID, and survey weights are not used as predictors. Leaving out country lets the model be applied to countries it was not trained on.

As noted above, the two main types of preprocessing are `step_impute_median()` and `step_impute_KNN()`. Imputing the nearest neighbor is most appropriate for our analysis, as it will ensure that the observations being imputed are close geographically. However, the trade off is that it takes an extremely long time.

We are using logistic regression and LASSO regression as two algorithms to see if there are notable differences. The LASSO hyperparameter is Lambda via a tune grid to see if there are variables resulting in a heavy penalty or with no predictive power.

**Interpretation**

**a. What the results mean and whether the model is useful**

**What we estimated.** Our first model predicts whether a child is stunted using only the 16 non-survey predictors: cluster location, elevation, urban/rural status, SPEI drought exposure in four time windows, and MapSPAM crop area within 10 km. We tuned an L1-penalized (lasso) logistic regression with stratified 10-fold cross-validation on the 127,615 training children. The best penalty was the smallest value in the grid (1e-10), and the seven smallest penalties gave virtually identical results. In practice the lasso did almost no shrinkage, and it set only spei_mean_yr2 and drought_share_yr1 to zero. With 16 predictors and more than 100,000 observations, there was little overfitting for the penalty to fix. The model's problem is a weak signal, not too much variance.

**How well it predicts.** The cross-validated ROC AUC is 0.611. If we pick one stunted and one non-stunted child at random, the model gives the stunted child a higher risk score 61% of the time, compared with 50% for a coin flip.

**Error rate in context.** In Question 1d we argued that false negatives (missing a stunted child) are the costlier error. To see what that means in practice, we examined out-of-fold predictions from the current median-imputation version of the model on the same ten folds. That version's AUC is 0.612, matching the saved run.

**Is the model useful?** As a child-level screening tool, no. Its discrimination is poor, and no cutoff gives an acceptable trade-off: it either misses most stunted children or flags most children, which adds little over screening everyone.

The case for the model is at the area level. Its inputs come from GPS coordinates and public climate and crop rasters, so it can be computed for places and years with no household survey. That matters because DHS surveys happen only every few years, and routine growth monitoring has poor-quality weight and height measurements and low coverage.

**b. Next steps: feature engineering and modeling options**

**Feature engineering 1: Remove overlapping climate and crop variables, and combine the drought windows.**\
Many of our non-survey predictors measure nearly the same thing. In the training data, crop_ha_mean and rainfed_ha correlate at 0.99, and crop_ha_mean and staple_ha_mean at 0.91. Each SPEI average correlates at about −0.8 with the drought share for the same window. We would keep only crop_ha_mean and the four drought-share variables, and drop the rest. We would also add one summary variable, drought_first2yrs, built with mutate() and rowMeans(..., na.rm = TRUE) as the average drought share across the pregnancy, first-year and second-year windows.

**Feature engineering 2: Turn child age into age groups.**\
When we add the survey predictors in Models 2 and 3, child age will be one of the most important variables, but its relationship with stunting is not a straight line. A logistic regression that treats age_months as a single number can only fit risk that steadily rises or steadily falls with age, so it misses any steep climb or sharp decline. We would create an age_group variable with case_when() (0–5, 6–11, 12–23, 24–35, 36–47 and 48–59 months) and let step_dummy(), which we already use, turn it into indicator columns.

**Modeling option 1: A random forest with mostly default settings.**\
The lasso chose essentially no penalty, which tells us our linear model is too simple for the data, not too complex. A random forest builds many decision trees on random samples of the data and averages their predictions. That lets it pick up curved relationships and combinations of variables, such as drought mattering more in rural areas, without us writing them into the formula. It also needs little setup. It doesn't require standardized predictors, and the defaults (about 500 trees) usually work well, so we would tune only mtry and min_n over a small grid.

**Modeling option 2: Use a lower cutoff and judge the model by how many stunted children it catches.**\
Right now the model labels a child as stunted only when the predicted probability is above 0.5. An interesting idea is to try a few lower cutoffs, such as 0.40, 0.32 and 0.25.. We would pick the cutoff that reaches a target sensitivity, such as 80%, and report how many children it flags, so a program can judge whether it has the capacity to follow up with them.
